function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends an HTTP GET request to retrieve Device Connector Versions information from a specified URL. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. The URL points to a JSON file containing Device Connector Versions information.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the GET request as key-value pairs.

message.content:
Below is a quick‑start cheat sheet you can copy into your terminal / console or adapt to scripts/automation.  
It covers:

| Platform | Tool | Command | What it shows |
|----------|------|---------|---------------|
| **Linux** | `ip` | `sudo ip -d link show <iface>` | All low‑level details – MTU, flags, driver state, TX/RX queues, offload settings, hardware addresses, statistics… |
|          | `ethtool` | `sudo ethtool -i <iface> && sudo ethtool -S <iface>` | Driver name/version + per‑interface counters & capabilities. |
|          | `ss` | `ss -tulnp sport = :<port>` | Which sockets belong to this iface (useful when filtering traffic). |
| **macOS** | `networksetup` | `/usr/sbin/networksetup -getinfo "<Service Name>"` | Service name → IPv4/IPv6, DNS servers, gateway, DHCP lease data. |
|           | `ifconfig` | `ifconfig <iface>` | Classic output – flags, HW/MAC, inet(4)/inet6, broadcast, netmask, tx/rx bytes. |
| **Windows** | PowerShell | `Get-NetIPConfiguration -InterfaceAlias '<Name>'` | Full IP configuration plus DNS, routes, gateways. |
|             | PowerShell | `Get-NetAdapterStatistics -Name '<Name>'` | Tx/Rx packet counts, errors, collisions. |
|             | CMD | `wmic nic where NetEnabled=true get *` | Hardware properties, speed, media type, GUIDs. |

---

### Example usage

#### Linux (`eth0`)
```bash
$ sudo ip -d link show eth0
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,RUNNING,PROMISC,VLAN_MTU> mtu 1500 qdisc mq state UP mode DEFAULT group default 
    link/ether aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    altname enp1s0f0
    qosid 0
    arp valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
```

```bash
$ sudo ethtool -i eth0
driver: e1000e
version: 7.3.21-k8-NAPI
firmware-version: N/A
bus-info: 0000:03:00.0
supports-statistics: yes
supports-test: no
supports-eeprom-access: no
supports-register-dump: no
supports-priv-flags: no
```

```bash
$ sudo ethtool -S eth0 | grep rx_packets
rx_packets               : 12345678
tx_packets               : 87654321
...
```

#### macOS (`en0`)
```bash
$ /usr/sbin/networksetup -getinfo Wi-Fi
Device Address:   AA-BB-CC-DD-EE-FF
DHCP Server:      192.168.1.1
DNS Servers:      192.168.1.1
Subnet Mask:      255.255.255.0
Router:           192.168.1.254
Primary Domain:   
Secondary Domains:
```

#### Windows PowerShell (`Ethernet`)
```powershell
PS C:\> Get-NetIPConfiguration -InterfaceAlias Ethernet

InterfaceIndex        : 12
InterfaceAlias        : Ethernet
ConnectionState       : Connected
DhcpServer            : 10.0.0.1
IPAddress             : {10.0.0.5}
PrefixLength          : 24
Gateway                 : 10.0.0.1
DNSServer              : {10.0.0.53}

PS C:\> Get-NetAdapterStatistics -Name Ethernet
BytesReceived         : 1023456789
PacketsReceived       : 98765432
ErrorsIn              : 0
...

```

---

### Automating the collection

If you’re writing a script that needs to pull all those fields programmatically:

* **Python/Linux** – use `subprocess.run(['ip', '-j', 'link', 'show', iface])`
* **PowerShell** – `$stats = Get-NetAdapterStatistics -Name $iface; $conf = Get-NetIPConfiguration -InterfaceAlias $iface`
* **Go** – call `golang.org/x/net/bpf` or invoke system utilities through `os/exec`.

For remote devices that expose SNMP, look up the standard MIB objects:

| Object | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| IF-MIB::ifDescr | Interface description |
| IF-MIB::ifPhysAddress | MAC address |
| IF-MIB::ifOperStatus | Operational status |
| IF-MIB::ifHCInOctets / ifHCOutOctets | High‑capacity byte counters |
| IF-MIB::ifSpeed | Link speed |

Use an SNMP client such as `snmpwalk -v2c -c public host .1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1`.  

--- 

That’s basically everything you’ll ever need to “dig deep” into a single interface across major platforms. Happy probing!
